mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares the nucleophilicity of I⁻ and Br⁻ in protic and aprotic solvents?

options.A: In both protic and aprotic solvents, I⁻ is a stronger nucleophile than Br⁻.
options.B: In a protic solvent I⁻ is a stronger nucleophile than Br⁻, whereas in an aprotic solvent Br⁻ is stronger than I⁻.
options.C: In a protic solvent Br⁻ is a stronger nucleophile than I⁻, while in an aprotic solvent I⁻ is stronger.
options.D: The nucleophilicity of I⁻ and Br⁻ is independent of the solvent.

mcqs.answer: In a protic solvent I⁻ is a stronger nucleophile than Br⁻, whereas in an aprotic solvent Br⁻ is stronger than I⁻.
mcqs.explanation: In protic solvents larger, more polarizable ions are less strongly solvated, so nucleophilicity follows size: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. In aprotic solvents solvation is minimal, and nucleophilicity follows basicity: F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻. Hence the correct comparison is given in option B.

mcqs.question: When chloromethane (CH₃Cl) undergoes homolytic cleavage of the C–Cl bond under ultraviolet light, which pair of species is formed?
mcqs.explanation: Homolytic fission splits a covalent bond such that each atom retains one of the shared electrons, producing two radicals. UV light provides the energy to break the C–Cl bond of CH₃Cl, yielding a methyl radical (CH₃·) and a chlorine radical (Cl·). Options A and B describe heterolytic cleavage, while D is unrelated.

mcqs.question: Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond results in which of the following?

options.C: Two ions of the same charge

mcqs.explanation: In heterolytic cleavage the two bonding electrons go to one atom, producing a positively charged ion (cation) on the other atom and a negatively charged ion (anion) on the atom that receives both electrons. This is the defining feature of heterolytic fission.

mcqs.question: Which of the following best defines a free radical in organic chemistry?

options.A: A neutral molecule that possesses an even number of electrons
options.B: A species that contains an unpaired electron
options.C: A positively charged ion formed by loss of an electron
options.D: A species that has a complete octet and no charge

mcqs.answer: A species that contains an unpaired electron
mcqs.explanation: A free radical is characterized by the presence of an unpaired electron, making it highly reactive. Options A and D describe stable molecules, while C describes a cation, not a radical.

mcqs.question: Carbocations are best described as:

options.A: Neutral carbon atoms bearing a lone pair of electrons
options.B: Positively charged carbon atoms with an empty p orbital
options.C: Negatively charged carbon atoms possessing a lone pair
options.D: Carbon-centered radicals with an unpaired electron

mcqs.answer: Positively charged carbon atoms with an empty p orbital
mcqs.explanation: Carbocations carry a positive charge on carbon and have an empty p orbital, making them electron‑deficient. Option A describes a neutral nucleophile, C describes a carbanion, and D describes a radical.

mcqs.question: Which of the following species is a carbanion?
mcqs.explanation: A carbanion is a carbon atom bearing a negative charge and a lone pair of electrons. CH₃⁻ fits this definition. CH₃⁺ is a carbocation, CH₃· is a radical, and CH₂=CH₂ is a neutral alkene.

mcqs.question: Which reagent acts as the electrophile in the electrophilic aromatic substitution of benzene to give nitrobenzene?
mcqs.explanation: In the nitration of benzene, the active electrophile is the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) generated from HNO₃/H₂SO₄. NO₂⁻, Cl⁻, and OH⁻ are nucleophiles, not electrophiles, in this context.

mcqs.question: In the SN2 reaction of ethyl bromide (CH₃CH₂Br) with aqueous NaOH, which species acts as the nucleophile and what is the major product formed?

options.A: OH⁻ is the nucleophile; product is CH₃CH₂OH
options.B: Br⁻ is the nucleophile; product is CH₃CH₂Br
options.C: Na⁺ is the nucleophile; product is CH₃CH₂Na
options.D: CH₃CH₂Br is the nucleophile; product is CH₃CH₂OH

mcqs.answer: OH⁻ is the nucleophile; product is CH₃CH₂OH
mcqs.explanation: In an SN2 mechanism, the hydroxide ion (OH⁻) attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing the leaving group (Br⁻). The bromide leaves, and the product is ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH). Br⁻ is the leaving group, not the nucleophile, and Na⁺ does not participate in bond formation.
